utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Gerguri, yesterday during cross-examination by Mr. Milosevic and again during questioning by Mr. Tapuskovic, you mentioned that NATO planes dropped bombs on or near the village of Lakovica in the municipality of Vushtrri. Approximately, if you know, on what date did the NATO planes bomb Lakovica?

utterances.speaker: MEHDI GERGURI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date. It was about -- about the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So that would be about 12 or 13 days after you were wounded in the large convoy that left the village of Studime e Eperme on the 2nd of May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHDI GERGURI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Gerguri, to your knowledge, before the 2nd of May, 1999, did NATO planes bomb anywhere else close to your village of Studime e Eperme?

utterances.speaker: MEHDI GERGURI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, before the convoy began to move away from your village of Studime e Eperme, did you see any NATO planes or any other planes dropping any bombs?

utterances.speaker: MEHDI GERGURI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, 1999, after the convoy left the village of Studime e Eperme, did you see any NATO planes or any other planes dropping any bombs?

utterances.speaker: MEHDI GERGURI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anything of that kind. Movements in the air, but there was no bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: While you travelled in that convoy, did you hear or feel any explosions caused by bombs dropped from the air?

utterances.speaker: MEHDI GERGURI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I was wounded. I wasn't able to see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Moving on to another topic, Mr. Milosevic suggested that there might have been more than two KLA members travelling in that convoy on the 2nd of May, 1999, and he read you the names of some people who were allegedly part of the KLA units in that area. Tell me, when the Serb forces attacked your part of the convoy, did any of the Serb forces attempt to search your tractor and trailer for weapons or for KLA members?

utterances.speaker: MEHDI GERGURI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't search anything. They just killed people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At that time, did any of the Serb forces ask you or anyone else near you for your name or your identity documents?

utterances.speaker: MEHDI GERGURI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't ask me anything like that. They just asked for money from me. I gave them money and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Serb policeman who ordered you to get off your tractor and give him money, did he ask to see your identity documents?

utterances.speaker: MEHDI GERGURI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just money. He didn't ask for any documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before this policeman shot you, did he search your tractor or trailer?

utterances.speaker: MEHDI GERGURI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Gerguri, did this policeman or any other member of the Serb forces that you saw on the night of 2nd of May, 1999, show any interest at all in determining which persons in the convoy were civilians and which persons in the convoy might have been members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MEHDI GERGURI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Gerguri, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I propose the next witness to be Dr. Liri Loshi. He is a 92 bis witness, however, I will be requesting leave of the Court to expand the summary by adding a slightly less than four-minute videotape that has been the subject of comment, and we have edited a tape that was over an hour to less than four minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. There's been examination about that tape from other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Exactly, so I'm seeking leave of the Court to play that at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, it might be convenient, while we're waiting for the witness, to deal with various other applications which have been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There will be leave to call Mr. Stijovic and Mrs. Simic. Both of those deal with relevant matters. There will be leave to admit Fetije Imeraj under Rule 92 bis. She deals with matters which have been in evidence to do with Padaliste. However, there will have to be cross-examination were her evidence to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Dr. Loshi, do I understand correctly, sir, that you are a medical doctor who lived in the area of Izbica during March of 1999 and that it's your familiarity with what happened in that area that brought you to court today?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you attend Izbica on the 31st of March, 1999, and did you participate in identifying the victims and videotape the scene of the massacres of the 28th of March at Izbica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, do I understand that you are currently 42 years old, that you are of Kosovo Albanian Muslim background, and you're originally from the village of Padaliste; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, prior to the conflict, how long had you practised medicine?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Before the conflict started, I had been involved in medicine for about eight to ten years. And if you add the two years of the war, that makes ten years in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just a couple of other questions by way of preliminaries, sir. Do I understand, sir, that you moved from your home in June of 1998, and can you tell us very briefly why it was that you did not continue to move -- to live in your home in June of 1998.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I didn't stay in my own home because it had been burnt round about 15th of June, and I had nowhere to live. The other thing was that in my village, after my house was burnt, there were various other houses burnt. I was in great danger because the asphalted road over which the Serbian military forces passed was very close to the village, and in fact passed by the village, so it was very dangerous for me to continue my work as medical doctor in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Very briefly, I understand, sir, that after your home was burned, you then travelled around in the area and lived with friends in other villages, practising medicine in the various small villages in the Srbica/Skenderaj area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you give statements to investigators of the ICTY on both the 19th of May, 1999, the 22nd of May, 1999, and then again statements on the 25th of September, 2001?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And, sir, did you also appear before an officer of the Tribunal on the 18th of June, 2002, review those statements in your native Albanian language, and confirm that the contents of those statements were true and accurate to the best of your information and belief?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might those statements, the bis'ing package as we call it, Your Honours, be given an exhibit number and entered into evidence at this time. And perhaps if we could get a number, then I'll start reading while they're being distributed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 307 for the original, under seal, and Prosecutor's Exhibit 307A for the public redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. With the Court's permission, I'll read while that's being handed. Your Honours, the witness describes in his statements how various villages in the area around Srbica were attacked by Serb forces on various dates in March 1999 and notes that by the 25th of March, thousands of refugees had assembled in an open field in Izbica. He heard about the massacre in Izbica by speaking to some of the women who were forced to leave. The witness's statements indicate that on the 31st of March, 1999, he subsequently attended Izbica along with Sefedin Thaci and others, where he assisted in the recording of a videotape of the bodies found in the village of Izbica. The video camera was operated by Sefedin Thaci under instruction from Dr. Loshi. The original videotape was apparently handed over by the witness to an investigator, Tait-Harris, of the ICTY while he was in Tirana, Albania, on the 18th of May, 1999. The witness, in his statement, explains how the video was made and states that this tape was the original version and had not been edited, added to, or altered in any way. The witness relates that the tape was filmed showing most of the bodies in the locations that they were found. The tape shows their faces, where possible, for identification purposes, together with the injuries on the bodies. The tape also shows the size of the burial site and depicts three of the survivors re-enacting the massacre to illustrate what took place. The statement describes in detail what is shown on each relevant frame of the video, the name of the victim where known, and describes the clothing worn. On the 22nd of May, 1999, in Tirana, Albania, the witness handed over to investigator Kevin Curtis a list detailing the names of the 127 people buried in Izbica which had been compiled with the assistance of Afrim Xhemajli. Now, during the course of this evidence, the witness -- we will also be asking to mark a videotape which bears a number V000-1733. From this videotape, still photographs were produced showing both the massacre scenes and the bodies. They are contained in the Izbica binder which has been made available to Your Honours and has been marked as an exhibit. In addition, the Prosecution has now edited that tape to show approximately slightly less than four minutes out of Exhibit 1733, to show highlighted portions of the video. I propose to show the witness this four-minute tape, and it shows four - and I'm now told actually five - scenes. The first scene shows the first group of victims where they were found. And I pause here to say you've heard one witness who testified about that first group. Then there is a short break in the film, purposely to separate the scenes, and we then see the second group of victims - and I pause here to say that you've also heard a witness who testified about being a survivor of that second group - followed by a brief view of the large meadow where the people had been assembled. You will then see the remnants -- you will see the remnants of the tractors and the debris left behind. The tape then pans to the third group of victims; and also at the very end, there's a very small segment of the actual burial site. All that is still within four minutes. Now, Your Honours, I could play the tape here, but I think I will finish with the summary, if I may. The witness also explains in his statement that while in Tirana, Albania, he was contacted by an American organisation called Witness, a human rights organisation based in New York. They provided him with a digital video camera and asked him to produce film for them upon his return to Kosovo. He returned to Kosovo on the 22nd of June, 1999, and attended the village of Padaliste in the municipality of Istok on the 24th of June, 1999 where he went to the house of Bek Imeraj. He was accompanied by Zenel Loshi, a cousin; a Xhavit Dragaj from Lecina; Ramadan Dragaj, a KLA soldier also from Lecina. Seven badly decomposed bodies were found in and around the yard of Bek's house which he then videotaped using the digital video camera. The witness also visited and videotaped the house of Daut Imeraj and Zenun Imeraj, whose wives were killed. On the 25th of September, 2001, the witness handed over to investigator Dagsland of the OTP that original videotape pertaining to the Padaliste village. Again he indicates that it was not edited or altered in any way. I pause here to say, Your Honours, we had originally planned on putting that tape in through Dr. Loshi but you've already seen that during the evidence, I believe of Mrs. Imeraj, when we fast forwarded portions of it, you may recall that, just last week. So I believe it's already been made an exhibit. During proofing, Dr. Loshi explained that as a medical practitioner in the Izbica area, he knew and had treated some of the victims of the massacre in Izbica prior to the 28th of March, 1999. So he knew them. He had also treated some members of the KLA from time to time, and in August of 1998, he himself became a member of the KLA but did not personally participate in armed combat. At this point, Your Honours, I would propose to ask the video booth to play that edited tape that I have made reference to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We're now seeing, Your Honours, that first group of bodies. There's a break here, Your Honours, to distinguish the groups. Here's now the second group. This is the field, Your Honours, referred to, and you will see the debris and the burnt-out tractors and cars that are left behind after the 5.000 some-odd people left this area. Panning now to the third group. And finally, Your Honours, what I understand is a very brief overview of the scene where the burial took place. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Very briefly, Dr. Loshi, you've had an opportunity, as we all did, to see this very brief edited tape. Do you recognise the scenes from this edited video as being part of the videotape that you provided to investigators of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And although obviously very shortened, are these scenes that we have seen true and accurate depictions of what you saw on the days that you took the video?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Everything that was filmed was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Couple -- just a couple of other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ryneveld. Before we go on, that video should have a separate exhibit number if it hasn't one already.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. I propose that we mark it with an A following whatever number we -- no. I'm sorry. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I was under the impression we had already marked that original tape as an exhibit and we haven't, so please. We could mark the original tape as an exhibit and give a new number to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, a new exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 308.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Doctor, very briefly, from your experience as a medical doctor when you arrived on the scene, were you able to determine, just by looking at it, how these individuals met their death?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: First I must say that I talked to various women that I met in the village of Tushile where they had taken shelter and who had came with that group, having been divided from their husbands and with the wives of the executed men, and they had told me what had happened at Izbica. Then I went to two days later, on the 31st of March, and when I saw the bodies, I had in front of me -- I had -- I'd already had a conversation with the women, so it was more than clear to me that this had been a massacre committed by the armed forces, in this case the Serbian forces. However, also as a doctor, I could see that all the bodies filmed on the scene of the event where the execution took place, and you can see the manner in which they're dressed, their shoes which were not taken off at all; in other words, it's very clear that they went from one part of the village to the other. And I saw bloodstains at that same place where the bodies were, and the bodies were -- had signs of execution with gunshots. You could see from the appearance of their faces and other parts of their body that the -- they had been shot from very close range. This could be seen from the wounds on their faces, and their faces were generally totally destroyed and shattered as would happen from close-range fire. And I had no doubt, I had not a single doubt that all these bodies had been massacred by Serbian military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, just --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Dr. Loshi, I'm not asking you the -- who the perpetrators were. I'm simply asking you whether you could tell whether, for example, these people died as a result of drowning or as a result of gunshot wounds or -- that's what I'm after here. You've already told us you saw that they died from gunshot wounds; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. And from what you saw at the scene, could you determine whether these bodies appear to have died where they were -- where you saw them and videotaped them or did they appear to have been moved to that location or are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I replied to this question before, but I'll repeat this. I have no doubt that those bodies had been executed in the place where we found them and where we filmed them, as you see in the video. There was no sign to show that the bodies had been carried from one -- from another place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just one other question, Your Honours, that is not related to his statements but something that this witness may be able to assist, and I'll ask it now rather than wait for re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, did you know a Sadik Xhemajli?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And this Sadik Xhemajli, do you know whether or not he wore corrective lenses and whether or not Mr. Xhemajli's corrective lenses, well, actually looked like sunglasses or dark-coloured glasses? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I know. This person has trouble with one eye. In his left eye is damaged, and other eye problems, and so the doctor has prescribed glasses for him. And I know that this person wears glasses to protect him from the sun. And not only for functional reasons but also for the sake of appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Sir, to the best of your knowledge, does he wear those wherever he goes?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: All the time. Wherever he goes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Those would be the questions. I just wonder, Your Honours, that -- Your Honours appreciate that these are two separate tapes. The Izbica tape was taken at a different time than the Padaliste tape, which was marked earlier, and so they are two different massacre sites. And the other thing is that at the back of the bis package, there are apparently a couple of additional pages which were not intended to be part of it. They appear to be some pages which are part of the proofing binder which accidentally found their way into the bis'ing package, but they -- these are pages that refer to the witness's name but are not part of his statement. They are in, fact, pages of other witnesses' statements that make reference to it. So somehow they found their way into the bis'ing package, and I just thought I should bring that to your attention that they're really not his statement, they're statement of others. You can see that at the top of the pages, "Statement of" and then another name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't seem to have got that. It's not in my copy, but it may be several pages in from the back. But in any event, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are my questions of this witness at this time. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ryneveld explained that this witness - I wrote down exactly what he said - carried out the taping of the scene of the massacre of the 28th of March -- May. When did you tape this?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: This footage was filmed on the 31st of March and 1st of April of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you claim that the massacre took place on the 28th of March, and you claim that you taped this on the 31st of March, three days later, based on what you claim, that a massacre took place at all.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Based on what I've seen with my own eyes on the 30th of March in the evening, on the 31st of March and 1st of April, when we conducted the filming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You saw some dead people, but you don't know how they died. It is not in dispute that these people are dead, but it is in dispute how these people died. How do you know how they died?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: The database that I provided for this Court proves clearly that these people, not only they were dead but they had been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what this argument "proves clearly." What does that mean? I'm asking you: What are you basing your claims on, "the argument clearly shows"? What does it mean, "clearly shows"? This is not clear to me, for example.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Considering that I knew the circumstances of the period back then, since I was living in Izbica, and also I was very close to Izbica when the event happened and I was together with people who left on the very day of the massacre, that is, on the 28th of March. I contacted people who left the group where men, women, and children were together and where men were separated by women [as interpreted]. I was referring to the conversations I had with them, and my going to the village of Izbica two days later, on the 30th of March, and the views that I came across, what I saw, I saw that they corresponded with the accounts of the women who had been separated from the group and had told me. I verified that these bodies had been shot and all these persons had been shot by the Serb military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well, Mr. Loshi. That's where we are. You are proving this through some circumstances that you are claiming, through something that happened. And how does this look, these circumstances? Let me read your statement. On page 3, you claim that on the 20th of March, 1999 -- this is the third passage on the third page in the Serbian version. "On the 20th of March, 1999, members of the Serbian army, police, and paramilitaries surrounded the town of Srbica. During this action, I know that 16 civilians were killed in several incidents in the town." This is what you claim in your statement: Surrounded Srbica, incidents in the town, 16 civilians. And now may I read --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If it assists, page -- I believe page 3 of the 31-page statement, about halfway the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's the statement of - so we have it - the 23rd to the 25th of September of 2001. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is what you claim, and this is what happened on the 20th of March, 1999: "At 5.00 a.m., 20th of March, 1999, there are official reports and documents about this. At 500 hours, a terrorist attack was carried out from infantry weapons at the police station in Srbica against -- against members of the army of Yugoslavia. On that occasion, serious injuries were sustained by a police member, Zoran Rakocevic, born in 1967. He succumbed to these injuries and died the next day, on the 21st of March in the hospital in Pristina. And Zoran Gemaljevic, born in 1969, was lightly wounded."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you reading. This is cross-examination and not the reading into the record of events. You must ask the witness if he knows something about this before you go on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, if a very well-known incident, a terrorist attack on a police station --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. I'm going to stop you to stop the argument. Remember you're asking the witness questions. Now, ask him if he knows about the attack on the police station. If you don't, I will. And let's hear his account of it. He may know something about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this argument.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Judges Robinson and Kwon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Loshi, you've heard what the accused alleges; that there was an attack on the police station that morning. Now, can you assist us about that? Do you know anything about this attack? Can you confirm that such an attack took place or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot confirm such an attack having happened because, given all the information I had back then, and I mean on the 20th of March, the day when I contacted the people who had been displaced from the town of Skenderaj, I met those people in Turicevc where I was practising my profession as a doctor. I do not have the slightest bit of information or there was not even mention of an attack having been conducted by the Albanian army or something like that. All I know is that on the 20th of March, sometime before 5.00 -- or probably between the 19th and 20th of March, as soon as the Kosovo Verification Mission of the OSCE left Kosovo, the Serb forces came in and conducted this massacre on the civilian population, where 16 persons were killed, where, as I mentioned in my statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Loshi, I'm going to stop you now. We were dealing with the attack on the police station. Mr. Milosevic, he says he doesn't know. He can't confirm it. Now, it may be your case that there was such an attack on the police station and that this led to fighting. You can certainly put, of course, that there was fighting, but -- just a moment. Let me finish. But what you can't do is give a lot of evidence. It's the witness who is giving evidence at the moment, not you. Now, you can put questions to him, of course, but it's no good repeating that there was an attack on the police station; he can't confirm that. You can, in due course, put evidence in front of us about that. But go on asking him questions, of course, about what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Dr. Loshi -- just a second. Just a second, please. The events on 20th of March, 1999, is that what you heard from people rather than what you saw yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am based on what I have heard from other people. And on the same day, meaning the 20th of March, from people who were there on the critical day of the event. I was 12 kilometres -- approximately 12 kilometres away from Skenderaj, and that's how I could not have seen what happened with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Liri, I cited to you the event of the 20th of March in Srbica only because on the 20th of March you said that something quite incorrect happened in Srbica on the 20th of March. So at the same time and the same place that you're testifying about, I'm saying that what you are saying is not true. Are you deliberately making this up or did others tell you to do that, Mr. Liri?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I am mature enough to know that I do not need lessons from anybody in this case, I do not need suggestions from you. I am telling what I was told by people who saw this massacre with their own eyes, and this was simply a massacre on the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that there was no terrorist attack on the police station that day but there was a massacre of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: According to all the information that I collected and the conversations I have conducted with witnesses, I state that that day there was no attack whatsoever on the Serbian police station in Skenderaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Excellent. And let's go back to the video footage that you taped. You saw some people who are dead. I have many questions. How do you know that these people were not brought there? In your film footage, there are no pools of blood or anything like that around the dead bodies that you filmed. How can you prove that these bodies were not brought there?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: If one takes a careful look at them, bloodstains can be clearly seen in the places where we filmed the footage, meaning at the site where the dead bodies were lying. However, considering that only one day before that, that is on the 27th of March, I was in Izbica -- I mean, this is the date when I left Izbica, actually, and also considering the fact that I had contacted many of the people who I then found lying dead on the 30th of March in Izbica, how could I not assert that people had been shot in Izbica? And we found the bodies of people we used to know, and many of those people I recognised, and I used to know them before myself, personally. So I had a chance to spend time, and to me, the same people on the previous dates, 25th, 26th of the same month, and they're the same people who I found lying dead, shot in the same village two, three days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you very frequently use the word "clear" and obviously it's all very clear to you, it wasn't clear to others. For example, would you kindly comment the following as written by Jonathan Landy, staff writer of the Christian Science Monitor. He's talking about what Jan Bjorken [phoen] told him, an investigator of Amnesty International looking into Izbica, and he's saying the following: "[In English] Others recount how bodies of individuals killed around the area by Serbian police were brought to Izbica for burial. What is disturbing is that one person I talked to said they had buried the person who they named in Izbica, she continues, but I talked to another person who named the person, same person, and said, We buried him in the woods. Finally, she asks --" she meaning Jan Bjorken Amnesty International investigator -- asks, and again quotations: "People from the area, without direct knowledge, identified that as the location of a KLA graveyard. So it is tricky." [Interpretation] So those who investigated this event also, as you can see, had many questions. But let's come back to this. Let's not even say that in this article they're talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've told you this before: You cannot simply read things out and then move on as if you were giving the evidence. You're not giving evidence, you're asking questions. You must give the witness the opportunity to deal with that quotation that you read out from a journalist, Christian Science Monitor. Just let me finish. Now, Dr. Loshi, I don't know if you follow what was read out, but the suggestion seems to be that at least one person was moved and is described as being tricky and there was identification of the location of a KLA graveyard. You've heard that. This is what the journalist said. Is there any comment upon that that you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say that I personally have read different things about the Izbica case. I'm trying to give my comment on the question put by Mr. Milosevic and by yourself, Your Honour. I talked about the film made of the massacred bodies at the place of the incident, but I didn't say anything about the burial of the 127 bodies of whom I brought a list here to this court. And it has not been said that in this entire group of shot people, or who were killed in various ways, they were all from the three main groups that we've been talking about, which means that there were three groups of people shot, whom we saw with our own eyes and whom we filmed. And among these 127 people who were buried in the village of Izbica, there were also some individuals brought from other places. They had come from other places but they were still killed in Izbica. And as for the graveyard, it was the KLA graveyard. It was prepared in a mixed -- in a way which brought together members of the population and the KLA, because there were a very few number of people in this -- in Izbica at this time, and this involved a lot of cooperation between the KLA and the members of the civilian population in order to be able to bury the bodies, remembering that Serbian forces were still concentrated only one kilometre away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So that means that it was the KLA graveyard where members of the KLA were buried who had died in battle fighting our forces. And what then? So what? Where do you find your massacre there? Why did you think up the firing squad? You've thought that up, the liquidation, execution. It never happened. It never existed. Isn't that so, Mr. Liri?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I explained very clearly, and I can explain again, but I will not deal with these comments. My comment from everything that I have seen is that there was a massive murder of the civilian population there, of men mostly quite advanced in age. And it is not true that these were graves of the KLA in which the members of the KLA who were killed had been buried. It was a mass grave prepared by the civilian population, but I mentioned the army too because this was an operation to bury all these victims within two days with the dignity that they deserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liri, this endless repetition of lies won't give you the truth in the end. Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is also a comment. Now, you've put it to him that he's lying. He's dealt with it. Let us move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is a basic issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have just said that a massacre was committed there. Now, did you see that massacre take place? Did you see any execution take place there? What are you testifying about at all? You say that you got there three days later and filmed some dead bodies in a field, in a meadow. Did you see how those people were killed?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I said that I saw the killed people two days later. And on the third day, we started with the filming, the identification, and the burial. I explained very clearly what I saw with my own eyes. I didn't see the moment of execution because if I had, I would have been among them, and I would have been buried with them, and I wouldn't be able to testify in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, come on. Well, Milazim Thaci, who you yourself mentioned -- you mentioned Milazim Thaci yourself. He said here that he was shot from a heavy machine-gun but that God saved him. He had three bullet holes in his shirt and he said God saved him but not his shirt. And now you're mentioning him and bringing him up as a witness. As you can see, he himself says that he was there at the execution and that a heavy machine-gun targeted him from a distance of eight metres. Please, is it not logical that if you wanted to go to that particular spot three days later, that you went with a video camera to document what you found there? You took the camera with you to document the circumstances, right?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Would it be possible to have just the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question is: Did you, three days later when you went to Izbica, take with you a camera or, rather, did you arrange for this videotaping in order to document the event which you wished to document? Is that what you did?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: The filming of the footage from the Izbica massacre was not done by me alone. It was myself with Sefedin Thaci and with the assistance of the civilian population and members of the Kosovo Liberation Army. This was not my -- this was not an initiative of mine quite by chance. At the same time, I was working as a reporter for the Kosovo television channel, and during all the time, I had my own camera with me. However, on the 26th of March, my camera had been burnt, as I have mentioned in my statement as well. It was burnt in a house of the village of Lecina, where I used to live. And on the 30th of March, 1999, I did not have a camera when I went to the site of the event in Izbica. Therefore, we asked one of the villagers to provide a camera for us the next morning, and a friend of mine promised to bring one the next morning. So by the next day, we found ourselves a camera and proceeded with the filming. This is the truth about the camera and the filming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Loshi. My question was that if you wished to document the killing, the alleged killing of these people, and you mentioned 120 of them -- actually, there was a witness here and they didn't play his tape, he claimed there were 500 people, but that was, I suppose, for the Prosecution to save face, so they didn't want to play that tape. Now, you say 120 people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you make a recording? Why didn't you tape those people, those 120 people? On the tape, the video we were shown, we just saw three or four and they were taken close up so that we could see their faces. Isn't it logical, if you want to make a document of something, that you should have taped each of the 120 people on the spot where they were found in order to be able to establish what happened? Some of the shots were taken from very far off, and you can't even discern what they actually depict until you come close to. So you have several groups of dead bodies which you show which undoubtedly were brought in there to be buried the KLA cemetery because they had died previously, lost their lives fighting against our forces, so you have a recording of the funeral. And what does that prove? Just that you buried the dead. Are you proving anything else by that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What are you proving, except that dead bodies are being buried, with the tape that you made of the funeral -- of the burial.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: My answer is as follows: In the three groups that can be seen in the footage we just played here, it's not a matter of two or three bodies, as you say, but we are talking massive groups of people, big groups of people. And we are talking approximately 100 or more bodies which had been massacred in three groups, as seen. As I mentioned earlier, the other bodies that were found in the vicinity of the site where these three massive shot groups were found, we also filmed those. But the total of bodies, 127, if you look, if you watch my tape carefully, you can see that every single body is filmed and every single body is identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We're going to look at all that very carefully, don't you worry about that. And experts will take a look at that too, never you mind. But what I would like you to tell me is how, by showing a picture of a body in a meadow, you set out to prove that death was caused by execution. And then you go a step further and say that death occurred through execution and that the execution was carried out by the Serb army and police. How do you prove that by showing the picture of a dead body, of a dead man in a meadow?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Please. We're not talking about just one body. We're talking about 127 persons about whom I just spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what? You could have brought in 200 killed members of the KLA for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. I'm going to stop you. All this is argument. There's no point arguing with the witness. He's given his evidence. He's described what he filmed. There's no point asking him what it's supposed to prove. That's a matter which we're going to have to decide. You know this. You argue with witnesses and it's pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you were a doctor, a KLA doctor in that area, which KLA brigades engaged in battle during those days in that area? Are you going to tell us or are you going to say you don't know or keep quiet about it? Which KLA brigades engaged in fighting during those days in that region?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: There was no fighting of the KLA with Serb forces during those days. On the first day, that is on the day when the NATO bombing started, on the 24th of March, the Serb forces were concentrated in the asphalted road from Peja to Mitrovica, meaning from Rakosh, Padalishte, Citak, Junik, Vitak, Cubren, up until Klina, Brumen [phoen], Skenderaj. They started shooting towards the civilian population, and thus they also started surrounding the area. On the first day, the Kosovo Liberation Army resisted. However, considering that they had not adequate armament, not enough weapons - I mean the KLA - they had to withdraw, not only from the suburbs but also from Izbica where the civilian population reached 20.000 people, more than that. They wanted to make sure -- the KLA wanted to make sure the Serbs did not attack the civilian population. So in Izbica and around Izbica on the 25th, 26th, 27th, 28th of March, there was no fighting whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, I read out what actually happened on the 20th of March when, amongst other things, eight terrorists were killed in that attack. You're now claiming that there was no fighting. And I'm going to read an excerpt from a report, and there are documents about that, that on the 26th of March, from 16 to 1630 hours, in the village of Likovac, the Srbica municipality, a terrorist attack was launched against members of the Ministry of the Interior and that policemen were killed on the occasion. On the 26th of March, in fact. And that they were Milan Pavlovic, Dusan Trifunovic, Ljuboje Zivkovic, Dragivoje Gajic, Radisa Klikovic, and seriously wounded policemen were Ljubisa Razic, Dusko Gavrilovic, Milan Ilic, Veselin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You're not wasting the time of the Court like this. You are trying to read these documents. No doubt your purpose is to read them into the record in some way. You misunderstand the purpose of cross-examination. It is to cross-examine what the witness said, not to give evidence yourself. Now, unless you ask this witness some relevant questions, you're going to be stopped. Now, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did the witness say a moment ago that during those days, there was no fighting in that area? Isn't that what he said? He claimed that there was no fighting during those few days, and I am quoting from this report which says that on the 26th of March, there was fighting. And I go on to quote how many policemen were killed in that particular fighting. And how do you -- how many --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are you quoting from? What is the report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are official reports, Mr. May, official reports by the government of the Republic of Serbia, pertaining to the events that took place during those particular days. They are reports relating to those events, and I will tender them when the time comes. I'm just going to ask the witness now, because he claims that there was no fighting, whether there was in fact fighting. What I'm asking him is how many members of the KLA lost their lives in that particular region during those particular battles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, were 100 killed, the 100 that you buried, were they killed there and whom you are now representing as being civilians?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: First I will ask -- answer the question about the fighting between the KLA and the Serbian forces in Likovc. Mr. Milosevic, if you know well - and I suspect you do - the geography of Drenica, you will realise that there is no sense in your question because Likovc and Izbica are very far away. And there was no reason, if such things had happened at Likovc - and I'm not denying the possibility - there was still no reason for a massacre to happen at Izbica, because we are dealing with quite different activities by Serbian forces entering Izbica. They came from the other direction; from Padalishte, Runik, and Vitak and Citak, and not from Skenderaj and Likovc, the direction you talked about. And as for the number of KLA soldiers killed, I don't know exactly how many were -- soldiers were killed. Generally, soldiers were killed. But this has nothing to do with the massacre at Izbica, because in no place were 100 soldiers ever killed on one day. There were never such large numbers of soldiers killed on one day because the tactics of the KLA were more guerilla tactics. And there was never any confrontation, any frontal confrontation in which 100 soldiers could lose their lives in one day or one week. If 100 soldiers were to die, it would take months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, who claims that they were killed in one day, Mr. Loshi? Who says that they were killed in a single day and who says that they were killed in one particular spot? Is it true, Mr. Loshi, is it correct that you gathered up all the dead KLA members from the area in the course of those few days and buried them in one particular place, in one spot? Is that true, Mr. Loshi? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, this is not true. Nobody has ever argued this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I am bringing forth that assertion because it's true. And secondly, you say that that doesn't justify the massacre in Izbica. Of course, nothing justifies any massacre. What I'm saying is that you have conjured up that massacre in Izbica, that there was no massacre at all. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Thank you for honouring me with the word "fabrication," but everything that I have told is the truth, and there has been no fabrication at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true, Mr. Loshi, that you didn't see that at all? You never saw any massacre at all. Is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, he's accepted that. It's not part of his evidence that he saw anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let's move on according to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, you say at the end of the page that I've already quoted from where you state and claim that what happened happened on the 20th of March in Srbica, you say you went to Tusilje, and up until the 29th of March there were 30.000 people there. However, I wish to add that many KLA fighters stayed there, remained there because their families were there and they had to take care of their families. Tell me now, please, how many KLA fighters were mixed up amongst those civilians that you referred to that gathered in Tusilje, in the Tusilje area during those days? How many fighters fled and became mixed up with the civilians? How many of them were there? And you know that full well.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: In my statement, I have mentioned that in Tushile village, where there was a number of -- a big number of civilian population in order to defend themselves from the nature itself -- the nature of Serb bombing, and in order to be concentrated in an open field so that as soon as the Serb forces would come in, they would realise that they were nothing but civilian population and, therefore, they wanted to defend themselves from having what happened in Izbica happen to them too. I can tell you that initially there were KLA members there who were taking care of their families, but "taking care" in this case is in the sense of making sure that their family members were placed in an open area and then they all left. I mean, the KLA members sent their families to Tushile village and then left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. They left. Now, explain this to me: As one of the witnesses here -- and you have said that too, that there were some 20.000, et cetera, how is it possible that somebody can separate from 20 or 25.000 people just 120 males? Doesn't that seem to you to be illogical, that out of 20.000 people, only 120 of them should have been men?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No. On the day when men were separated from women, there were not 20.000 or 25.000 people there, even though this is a free interpretation. This is an assessment that one can conduct with the naked eye. However, on the day when men were separated from the women, there were between 3.500 or 4.000, maybe more, people. We do not have an exact figure but we know there were thousands of people. And it is known that all the men were separated and that was because the rest of the men had sought shelter in the mountains and were not together with the civilian population. I'm speaking about the vital part of it. Whereas the elderly stayed with the -- had stayed with the women and children, considering that the Serb forces wouldn't have anything to do with them. But their senses proved to be wrong and the total opposite of that happened. All of them were caught, and all of them, every single one of them, was shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The witness who was there, and that's not your case, you say you weren't there, Milazim Thaci, said that there were 15 or 16.000 of them in that meadow and that 140 were set aside, 140 men, and that all the men were set aside. And he said -- the figure he quoted was 15, 16.000. Now, you go on to say that as all the rest were women and the men were executed there, you say that "the women, of course, cannot confirm what happened exactly." Now, could you explain, please, why the women, of course -- these women "of course" could not confirm what had happened? Are they stupid or what? Do they not know? Why do you say "the women could, of course, not confirm what had happened" if they separated their menfolk, as you say, and executed them?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: As for the number, you remember 15, 16.000. This was a rough estimate of the population that had gathered initially on the 26th and 27th of March. And after that date, the larger part of this group had left and gone to Tushile, so that about 4.000, 5.000 people were left. Again, this is an estimate, because we didn't count them one by one. Meanwhile, as for the second part of the question as to whether the women could testify to this, I can say that from the conversations I had with the women on that day, we knew that they were sent away from the crowd forcibly, and they left in the direction of Turicevc and from there in two directions and went -- not went but were sent in the direction of Klina on the road to Albania, and it's said that this group suffered greatly because this group were -- had to go all the way to the border but were forced to go back, and the other group went -- of women went to Tushile to take shelter there, and I contacted this group and talked to them. So my conversation with them showed -- produced the information that their menfolk had been separated from them by force, and I heard how they were sent in two different directions but heard gunshots as they were going towards Turicevc. So the women were taken away from the men and they could not see the scene of the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, Mr. Loshi -- well, I understood that they were in the field and that they took the others several hundred metres towards the forest and that everybody could see. But tell me this: You say: "My part of the videotape begins with the scene where on the 31st of March the men are digging the graves," and there is a number on the camera as it records. That's not important. But let me ask you, when did that burial take place? They dug out the graves on the 31st of March, so was the burial and funeral on the 31st of March as well?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: The burial took place in Izbica in a valley between two hills that was concealed. In other words, it was invisible to the Serbian forces concentrated on the hills of the village of Vojnik, only one kilometre away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you when, Mr. Loshi.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: This happened on the 31st of March and 1st of April, 1999. In other words, we buried these bodies in the course of two days. There was a small number of people, a relatively small number of people who were able to participate in the burial. So we were unable to dig all the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Loshi, just -- if you would, just concentrate on answering the questions since time is short. Mr. Milosevic, we have to adjourn now. It's the time. You've had 50 minutes already. Are you asking for more time with this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am. I do need more time, Mr. May, and I would need quite a bit more time because here we see the whole fabrication of theirs about the Serbs and everything linked to those fabrications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll give you another quarter of an hour. So you should tailor your questions accordingly. Dr. Loshi, will you be back, please, in 20 minutes to conclude your evidence. Would you remember during the adjournment not to speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that does include members of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I looked at my notes. Fifteen minutes is not enough for me to put all the questions that I would like to put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've given our ruling. We've told you before, too much time is taken up with argument with the witness. If a witness doesn't agree with you, put your case to him and then move on and don't take up time arguing. But a quarter of an hour is the time we've allotted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at the end of the summer of 1998, in Turicevac where you were, between 400 and 500 members of the KLA were stationed who were armed with automatic rifles, machine-guns, mortars, recoilless cannon, and so on? Just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I must say merely that I don't know about the arsenal of weapons that you mentioned, but there were approximately that number of KLA soldiers present, not only in Turicevc but in the entire area covered by the 112th brigade. This was approximately the number of soldiers, but they mainly had light weapons, that is, automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement, and this is page 321, that's the last three digits, I'm quoting you: "Between the KLA and the Serbian forces, there were no major clashes. The KLA was not strong enough to in order to stand up to the Serb army and most frequently there were clashes with civilians." Why were there clashes with the civilians, could you please tell me, and why did the members of the KLA flee together with civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness answers that question, I think that the paragraph should be put to him fairly. Page 3 of 31. I'm asking you to read the third full paragraph that appears to be -- and from what I heard, the translation being read out, the quote put to him is not correct. That's not what the statement says, at least in the English version. The suggestion is that the KLA was not strong enough to resist the Serbian army and most of the time the suggestion was that they were clashing with civilians. That's not in this statement. Most of the time they were fleeing, as well as the population. That's what the statement says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can you deal with that, Dr. Loshi, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would just like to correct it. I don't know what you are quoting from, but this is page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not get the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and the quote precisely says: "There were no big clashes between the KLA," full stop. "The KLA was not strong enough to resist the Serbian army and most of the time they were fleeing with the civilian population." This is specifically what it states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The English is "as well as," but I don't think we need take further time on that. What was the question again, please, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked him to say what kind of clashes they were and why did members of the KLA flee together with the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: As I said before, the weapons of the KLA was -- was mainly light. And in comparison with the weapons of the Serbian army, this did not allow the KLA to conduct a frontal battle with Serbian forces. And so my statement that the KLA shirked clashes with the Serbian forces is accurate. However, there were battles, as I said, in using guerilla tactics that were employed by the KLA. But I did not say that the KLA and its members fled with the civilian population. They avoided conflicts not by fleeing with the civilian population but by concentrating on other areas, i.e., on the periphery in order to preserve the core of the KLA and not to give a pretext to the Serbian army and the Serbian military forces to commit crimes against the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [B/C/S translation on English channel] ... following. I think some people were killed. I think some people were killed and others were arrested. Are you testifying here about what you think or about what you know?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me and I don't remember in what way I said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: First of all, we are getting interruption on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked, Mr. May, him to explain what he said on page 3, and quoted. He said, "I think some people were killed and others were arrested." And I asked him, "Do you think that they were killed or do you claim that they were killed?" That the witness is testifying about what he claims and not what he thinks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must ask again an explanation for this question and its context, and what case are you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, whereabouts in the statement is it? We have the reference that you made to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 3, Mr. May. It says that he watched the village of Tusilje being shelled, and he says that some people were killed, but I find it hard now to find that because -- but the quote was correct in any case. I have no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that the question is now clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have the quotation. "On the 30th of March, I could observe green-coloured Serbian army trucks and tanks at the Vojnik hill. In the evening that day, the village of Tushile was shelled. I believe some people were killed and others arrested." Now, that's the relevant passage, and the question was: Is that true? Can you assist us to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how this phrase "I think" was put in. Perhaps it's a mistake that wasn't noticed by myself when I read the Albanian version, and perhaps the investigator used this word, but I have data to show that on the 30th of March, the village of Tushile was shelled and that Serbian forces entered, withdrew the civilian population, and scattered them in different directions. And at the same time, they took some men, a group of about 40 to 50 - I don't know the exact number - and as far as I know, the greater part of this group were released. I was able to contact some of these people because some of them, though not all, came to Izbica where some of them had their families. Because even after the massacre at Izbica, there was a considerable number of people sheltering in this village. So this statement is accurate, and so it's not a matter of theory or supposition but a truth that I learnt from people who had been present in Tushile. And as far as I know, again I say on the basis of conversations I had, 11 people were killed in Tushile village that day, but I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I want to be precise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found this in the statement, Mr. May. It's on page 4. It's the page which has the number 03035322, and it's the fourth passage, the last sentence. "In the evening that day, the village of Tushile was shelled. I believe some people were killed and others arrested." So this is the correct quotation. As you can see, it is quite correct. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement that the same evening, you went into the village of Tusilje together with your friends. I quote: "One of my friend was Shaban Dragaj, a KLA commander." Who were the other friends? Were they also members of the KLA or members of Shaban Dragaj's staff?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I have stated that in the mentioned date, I went to the site of the event with Shaban Dragaj, who was not only a member of the Kosovo Liberation Army but was also deputy commander and main chief of the 112th Brigade. In the meantime, I personally went with him and some other persons. I do not remember whether any of the other persons was a KLA member. However, it is possible that I may -- that any of them may have been a member of the headquarters. This is my answer as far as this question is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And you say in your statement, you explain that on the same night, you came to Izbica but that you were not able to see the bodies but you heard from the people what had happened, and then you said, "We decided to try to find a camera in order to document," et cetera, and this is what you showed to us, what you consider as documenting. My question is as follows: Was this Shaban Dragaj, the KLA commander, present with you all the time?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: If you mean the first night when we went together, then the answer is yes. During the whole time we were together and we saw the dead bodies, it was dark. We were not able to see the bodies clearly, but the truth is we did see them, and that is what I stated. I had remarks and personal observations about the reasons why we could not see the bodies. No. We could not see the bodies clearly. That is, we saw them. And Shaban Dragaj was with me during the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And after the 4th of April, when the tapes were -- after a few days, when they were re-recorded, you said the tape was stolen, you asked the commander for help, and it was confiscated from the thieves. Does that mean that the tapes were not in your possession or in the possession of the persons -- the person who taped them all the time? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: The truth is that the tape was obtained in an unfair way by some irresponsible person, and I asked for the assistance of the main chief of the brigade, Shaban Dragaj, who made sure, after a conversation with those persons, to have the tape back within a very short time. Meanwhile, as concerns the truth about the tape, it is true that this tape - I mean the original tape which I gave to the ICTY - was filmed with the camera of Sefedin Thaci while he himself was not present. In the meantime, I had my own tape which on the 4th of April I recorded from this original tape into VHS. And I had that tape all the time. But due to technical reasons, I left it somewhere in the mountains of Istok because it was very big, and I was thinking that there were chances that I could get caught by Serb forces and I didn't want the tape to be on me by then. And it was a wise thing to do to hide this tape. So that's why I took the other one, in order to use it for information purposes. In the meantime, as I said, I left the tape in the Istok mountains, and I then found it and brought it with me everywhere, and I've been carrying it with me everywhere I go all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Loshi. Could you please answer briefly because you are using up a lot of my time. Did you receive instructions from anybody about what and how to record?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: How could I receive these instructions when I filmed footage of the massacre of Izbica on the 31st of March, 1999, at a time when there were no foreign journalists present anywhere in Kosova or in the battlefields, not even where the massacres were taking place?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said, on page 03035323, I'm quoting you: "In the course of April, I received another videotape, and then on the 3rd I recorded some new scenes from Izbica." So these persons who gave you this new tape, and my question refers to them, did they give you instructions on how to tape? And what happened to that tape?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I am sorry, but I think you are mixing things. You're being confused. Before I left to Albania -- I left for Albania to give the tape where I filmed -- what I filmed, I had also filmed something on a tape of the same format as the previous tape which could also be used compatibly in every camera. That specific tape had new footage where one can see the burial site a month later. You can see the flowers and you can see the number of 107 tombs that had been dug a month ago. I was inside Kosovo in the meantime and I was not in contact with any kind of media whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not waste any more time with that. But please tell me, did you give that tape also to investigator Jonathan Harris? Just say yes or no without any long explanations.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Could you answer specifically to the question: Were the bodies moved?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were the dead bodies moved?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No. The bodies have been transported only when they were to be buried. All the bodies have been brought close to the cemetery in two places, and they have been identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've had another 20 minutes, which is more than we said you could have, but you can ask two more questions and then you must bring this to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, since they were not moved, why do you say in paragraph 4 that some were recorded two or three times and that they were moved to a place? And if you look at page 03035345, in paragraph 7, you say: "Some of the bodies were brought to the burial site from other locations. All of them were the victims of clashes, and we did not divide the bodies according to the place where they were killed." The point is as follows: They were all victims of clashes. That's what you said. "And we did not divide the bodies according to the place where they were killed."

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I have not said -- I have never said that all these victims, all of them were victims of clashes. We're not talking about victims of clashes. We're talking about innocent victims. Meanwhile, as concerns whether the bodies were moved, even though I gave an answer earlier, if you look at my earlier testimony today, I answered a very short while ago and I will repeat my answer. The bodies were moved from the place they had been executed only when we wanted to bury them and to identify them. Some of the bodies were identified during the filming of the site of the event, that is, where they were shot and died, whereas the rest was identified when they were lined up alongside the burial site, and we filmed footage of all of these moments. This is what I was referring to when I said what you are claiming that I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But, please, in your statement, you said that there were 127 victims and that you dug 127 graves and that they were all victims of clashes. Is this true or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, could you find this, please. It doesn't appear on any statement I have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I haven't been able to locate the exact quote either in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, where does it say this? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you look at page 28 of the English version, paragraph 3 from the bottom. So page 28 of the English version of the statement from the 23rd to the 29th, 2001, September 2001. So it's the third paragraph up from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we have it clear - thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic - the paragraph says this in the English: "Finally, I will say that I'm not quite sure how many of the 127 persons we buried at the gravesite actually were from the massacre. Some of these bodies were brought to the gravesite from other locations. They were all victims of the conflict, and we did not at that time categorise the bodies from where they were killed. However, the majority of the bodies came from the massacre when men were separated from women and children in the field outside Izbica on the 28th of March, 1999. I would estimate the number from the massacre to be between 110 and 120 persons." Now, that being the paragraph, Mr. Milosevic, this is your final question, what do you want to ask the witness about that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more question is not enough for me, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in these clashes that you mention incidentally here, during those actions -- I have a list of those who were killed. Thirty soldiers of the army of Yugoslavia, 25 police officers, all of them in your municipality during those clashes. And how can you say, then, that these were clashes in which the KLA did not fight, in which no one was killed. Thirty soldiers and 25 police officers. How many members of the KLA, then, were killed in those conflicts who, as you say, were much weaker in comparison to the regular army and police? And where did you bury them if not there?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: There are three different questions. I don't know which one to answer first. Could you possibly separate them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us get on with this. First of all, it's put that there were serious clashes, in effect, in which 25 police officers and 30 soldiers of the Yugoslav army were killed. Do you know anything about any such clashes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not denied, and I'm not denying now there have been clashes between the KLA and the Serb military forces. That is, the accused is referring to a whole region, to Drenica. However, he does not refer to Izbica and its surroundings. He does not mention even --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Liri, I must ask you just to deal with the questions, please. The next question is: How many members of the KLA were killed in the conflicts? Can you help with that? If you can't, how many do you know were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, from the beginning of the war until it was over, that is from the 24th, 25th, 26th, 28th of March, when the first fighting clashes occurred in Vojnik village, in Llausha, until the end of the war, approximately 200 soldiers of the KLA were killed. This is the period of time that was the beginning of the conflict, in fact, back in 1997. And the end of the war was in March --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't go back to that. You've dealt with the relevant period. The next question is: Where were they buried? Can you help us with that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were buried in the places where they were also shot. I don't know where each soldier was buried, but, for Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 9464 to 9475. example, if a soldier had been killed in my region, he would be buried in the village cemetery. If other soldiers had been shot in other villages, then that's where they would be buried. Therefore, there is no specific answer to where -- to who was buried where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
